title: Autumn Time in Four Countries
summary: See how autumn customs connect people with the moon, changing leaves, a large festival, and family members who have died. Compare the time, place, and meaning of each activity.

blocks.title: Introduction

blocks.title: Part 1: Moon Viewing in Japan
paragraphs: Autumn activities are easier to understand with three questions: When do they happen? Where do people spend time? What does the activity mean? We can use these questions in all four countries.

To see how people spend time in autumn in Japan, start with Tsukimi, the Japanese autumn moon-viewing custom. Jugoya is the fifteenth night of the eighth lunar month. In 2026, Tsukimi is on 25 September. People display dango, round rice dumplings, and susuki, or silver grass. The round dango stand for the full moon. The grass stands for rice and good crops.

images.alt: An adult woman in a peach cardigan stands on a wooden veranda at night looking at a bright full moon, with a pyramid of white rice dumplings and a vase of silver pampas grass on the railing; hands in pockets.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: Moon Viewing in Japan

items.prompt: What do the dango and silver grass mean in a Tsukimi display?
items.answer: The round dango stand for the full moon, and the silver grass stands for rice and good crops.

blocks.title: Part 2: Tsukimi in Daily Life
paragraphs: Now add place and daily routine to our three questions. Many people enjoy Tsukimi at home under the moonlight. It is a custom, not a national public holiday. There are no holiday days connected with the moon festival, so work continues as normal. Offices and shops stay open.

Businesses may still mark the season with special foods and marketing. This shows how a meaningful custom can be part of an ordinary working day. People do not need a whole day away from work to notice the season and enjoy the moon.

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: Tsukimi in Daily Life

items.prompt: Why can Tsukimi be part of an ordinary working day?
items.answer: Tsukimi is not a national public holiday, so offices and shops stay open and work continues as normal.

blocks.title: Part 3: Autumn Colour in Canada
paragraphs: In Canada, people spend time in autumn looking at fall colour and marking Thanksgiving. Fall colour means leaves changing colour in autumn. Algonquin Park, a large provincial park in Ontario, is one place where people can see this change.

The colour of Sugar Maple and Red Maple leaves is usually strongest in the last week of September or the first week of October. Canadian Thanksgiving is on the second Monday in October, and some park services stay open until that weekend. In our three-question lens, the place is a park, the time is early autumn, and the changing leaves are the main natural event.

images.alt: An adult man in a moss-green jacket stands at a wooden park overlook above a lake surrounded by red and orange maple hills, with a thermos on the rail; hands in pockets.

blocks.title: Check: Part 3: Autumn Colour in Canada

items.prompt: When is maple fall colour usually strongest in Algonquin Park?
items.answer: It is usually strongest in the last week of September or the first week of October.

blocks.title: Part 4: A Large Festival in Germany
paragraphs: In Germany, people spend autumn days at Oktoberfest, Munich’s big autumn festival. Munich is a city in Bavaria. The 191st Oktoberfest will take place at Theresienwiese, the festival ground in Munich, from 19 September to 4 October 2026.

This is a very large public event. About 6.5 million guests visited in 2025. Its history began with a royal marriage celebration on fields outside Munich on 12 October 1810. Horse races happened again the next year, and the event grew into Oktoberfest. Here, autumn time is spent in a busy public place rather than at home.

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: A Large Festival in Germany

items.prompt: How is Oktoberfest different from enjoying Tsukimi at home?
items.answer: Oktoberfest is a large public festival in Munich, while many people enjoy Tsukimi at home.

blocks.title: Part 5: Welcoming the Dead in Mexico
paragraphs: In Mexico, people spend time in autumn preparing for Día de Muertos, the Mexican Day of the Dead festivity. It happens each year from the end of October to the beginning of November. It marks the short return of family members who have died.

Families make an ofrenda, a home offering or shrine for the dead. They place favourite dishes, flowers, candles, and handmade objects around home shrines and tombs. Flower petals and candles can also mark paths. The period comes at the end of the yearly maize, or corn, growing cycle. UNESCO put this living tradition on its Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008.

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: Welcoming the Dead in Mexico

items.prompt: How does an ofrenda help families welcome the dead?
items.answer: An ofrenda welcomes the dead with favourite dishes, flowers, candles, and handmade objects.

blocks.title: Part 6: Comparing Autumn Time
paragraphs: Our three questions show important differences. In Japan, many people view the moon at home while normal work continues. In Canada, people look at changing leaves in places such as Algonquin Park and mark Thanksgiving. In Germany, people attend a large public festival in Munich. In Mexico, families prepare home shrines and tombs for relatives who have died.

The places are different: a home, a park, a festival ground, or a tomb. The times are also different, from late September to early November. However, each activity gives people a way to notice the autumn season and spend time with a custom, place, or memory.

images.alt: An adult woman in a peach cardigan and an adult man in a moss-green jacket walk a cobblestone street from warm festival tent lights toward a home doorway ofrenda with candles and marigold petals; all hands in pockets.

items.prompt: What three questions can help us compare these autumn activities?
items.answer: We can ask when they happen, where people spend time, and what each activity means.
